'''''Sisymbrium altissimum''''' is a [[species]] of ''[[Sisymbrium]]''. The plant is native to the western part of the [[Mediterranean Basin]] and is widely [[naturalized]] throughout most of the world, including all of [[North America]]. After maturity it forms a [[tumbleweed]]. Common names of the plant include '''Jim Hill mustard''', '''tall tumblemustard''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SIAL2|taxon=Sisymbrium altissimum|accessdate=16 November 2015}}</ref> '''tall mustard''', '''tumble mustard''',<ref name="Johnson1987">{{Cite book |title=Lubbock Lake : late quaternary studies on the southern high plains |publisher=[[Texas A&M University Press]] |year=1987 |isbn=0-89096-321-5 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Eileen |location=College Station |pages=29}}</ref> '''tumbleweed mustard''', '''tall sisymbrium''', and '''tall hedge mustard'''.<ref name="Royer&Dickinson">{{cite book |last=Royer |first=France |title=Weeds of the Northern U.S. and Canada: A Guide for Identification |author2=Richard Dickinson |date=1999 |publisher=[[The University of Alberta Press]] |isbn=978-1-55105-221-2 |pages=470}}</ref>

==Description==
Tumble mustard forms an upright but delicate-looking plant, with slender, much-branched stems, growing up to {{Convert|5|ft|abbr=off|order=flip}} in height. Its stem [[leaves]] are divided into thin, linear lobes, while the basal leaves are broader and pinnately compound. The flowers are inconspicuous and only {{Convert|1/4|in|abbr=off|order=flip}} wide. They have four usually yellow petals and four narrow, curved sepals. The seedpods are slender and long ({{Convert|5-10|cm|abbr=out|disp=or|frac=4}}). The plant [[germination|germinates]] in [[winter]] or early [[spring (season)|spring]], with a lengthy blooming period. At maturity it dies, uproots, and [[Tumbleweed|tumbles]] in the wind, spreading its seeds.<ref>{{cite book |author=Laird R. Blackwell |title=Wildflowers of the Eastern Sierra and adjoining Mojave Desert and Great Basin |year=2002 |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing |isbn=978-1-55105-281-6}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The [[common name]] 'Jim Hill mustard' is after [[James J. Hill]], a [[Canadian-American]] [[railroad]] [[magnate]], due to a farmers' [[tall tale]] about the seeds having been spread via his railroads.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
The plant is native to the western part of the [[Mediterranean Basin]] in [[Europe]] and [[Northern Africa]] and is widely [[naturalized]] throughout most of the world, including all of [[North America]].<ref name="Royer&Dickinson" /> It was probably introduced into North America as a [[weed control|contaminant of seed crops]].{{citation needed|date=June 2022}}

== Ecology ==
The plant grows in [[soils]] of all [[wikt:texture|textures]], even [[sand]].

== Uses ==
The leaves are spicy enough to make [[wasabi]] but can also be mixed into salads and other dishes.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>
